accuracy.evidence: Matches the research record: Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer (1993) linked top violinists to accumulated solitary practice aimed at weaknesses, Ericsson and Pool (2016) called the 10,000-hour rule a misreading, and Macnamara et al. (2014) found deliberate practice explained about 26% of variance in games, 21% in music and far less in education and professions. The lab models are labelled as toy models in the source.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs students bring: that hours alone make you expert, that a plateau means a talent limit, that always scoring 100% means practice is working, that the hardest material teaches most, that replaying a whole piece or paper fixes its weak part, that late feedback is as good as fast, and that you can fix eight problems at once or practise well while distracted.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagdelib lab shares no activity with the spacing, retrieval or younger practice labs: a 20-week two-player skill chart, a six-bar piece with a budget of six loops where the whole piece is capped by its weakest bar, a difficulty dial showing success rate against learning per session, a blind-then-visible aiming drill with a hidden drift, and a plan sort. It passed the shingle check against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each principle is felt before it is named. The learner watches Ana level off near 60 while Ben reaches 79 on the same hours, runs out of loops if they polish strong bars, sees learning peak at a 62 to 82% success rate, and fires three shots blind before feedback reveals the up-right drift they then correct by moving the aim.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions each carry a tempting wrong option: same hours means same result, playing the whole piece six times, work you always get right teaches most, and 100 shots will improve you even without seeing where they land. The learner's guess is played back next to the outcome after each task, so the gap between belief and result is explicit.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions, every wrong option tagged with its own feedback: hours (time alone), talent (plateau as a fixed limit), easy (comfort zone), hard (panic zone), whole (replaying everything), late (slow feedback), focus (half attention) and all (fixing everything at once). Each message names the principle and refers back to the lab, such as Ana and Ben's equal hours.

readability.evidence: The learner kid text scores about grade 3.5 and the adult text about grade 7.5 on Flesch-Kincaid, well inside the learner limits, without dumbing down for 16 to 17 year olds. Terms such as stretch zone, comfort zone, naive practice, metacognition and meta-analysis are explained in plain words where they first appear, and lab steps have one instruction each.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a finding, a method or a named mistake. The adult text cites the 1993 violin study, the 10,000-hour misreading, the 2014 meta-analysis limits and the EEF metacognition guidance, then turns them into concrete steps: use mock results to find the weakest topic, set work at 60 to 85% right, mark straight away and fix one thing at a time.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop in the browser gate. The chart scrub, difficulty dial and aim crosshair all use A.gest so touch and mouse both work, and each drag has button alternatives (Next 4 weeks, Easier and Harder, arrow nudges and Shoot), with bars and bins sized for a thumb on a 360 px wide screen.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reported no violations in light or dark theme. The canvas aria-label is updated with every result, all numbers such as skill scores, bar percentages and hits are written as text rather than shown by colour alone, every control is a labelled button, and lab colours come from A.col so contrast holds in both themes.

sources: Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T. and Tesch-Römer, C. (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review 100(3), 363-406
Ericsson, A. and Pool, R. (2016) Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise (purposeful versus naive practice; critique of the 10,000-hour rule)

Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z. and Oswald, F. L. (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis. Psychological Science 25(8), 1608-1618
Education Endowment Foundation (2021) Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (plan, monitor, evaluate)
